title: Morphic fields as memory
content_html:
Morphic fields as memory

Rupert Sheldrake’s proposal of morphic fields and morphic resonance is one of the best-known attempts to frame field theory as collective memory. Morphic fields are invisible organizing fields that shape the form and behavior of biological systems, ecosystems, and even social groups. The hypothesis is that once a form or behavior has happened, it becomes easier for it to occur again — because a “memory” has been imprinted in the field. This implies that memory is not stored in the brain alone but exists as part of a larger, field-like structure that connects individuals and species.

For Sheldrake, memory is non-local; the brain is not a storage device, but a tuning system that “taps into” morphic fields, so individual recall is seen as resonance with a collective past. This challenges the dominant neuroscientific model, where synaptic changes encode memory locally. Learning spreads not only genetically but via resonance; if one population acquires a new behavior, others may pick it up more easily. This is cultural transmission: traditions and habits persist because the field “remembers” them, which casts tradition, habit, and archetype as field phenomena, not just cultural constructs.

There are parallels in other theories: Carl Jung’s collective unconscious in which archetypal memory is shared across humanity; David Bohm’s implicate order where the universe enfolds and unfolds patterns of information. Even without strong empirical support, Sheldrake’s model is philosophically stimulating because it expands the idea of memory beyond the neural substrate and resonates with ecological and relational views of mind.

Dependent origination

In Buddhism, nothing exists independently; all phenomena arise in dependence on conditions (causes, context, relationships). This is not a “thing” or “field” but a principle of conditionality: everything is co-arising, mutually influencing, without inherent existence. The idea of a ‘non-local field’ is not completely different, in that it describes patterns of relation rather than isolated entities, so that what happens in one place/time can’t be understood without wider conditions, resisting the idea of a purely local, atomistic storage of memory or identity. However, Buddhist dependent origination is not a substrate, it is not a hidden field that transmits information across space/time. Instead it describes the logic that whatever arises does so in dependence on causes and conditions. Memory, in this view, is conditioned by brain, body, environment, cultural practices, karmic tendencies — all interdependent.

For Buddhism, interdependence works without postulating a new medium, the interconnection is direct, not via a field in between. The implication is that non-locality is already built into the structure of reality: everything is co-arising, not because a field carries it, but because nothing ever arises apart from conditions. When modern readers hear “dependent origination,” it can be tempting to imagine a field of relations that “remembers” or “connects” phenomena. Just as Sheldrake’s morphic fields are habits that link instances, dependent origination describes causal patterns that ripple through conditions, giving a sense of continuity without fixed essence; it is closer to a causal law of radical interdependence. But if you translate it metaphorically, it resonates with the intuition that memory, mind, and form are not self-contained but emerge from an unbounded web of relations.

Morphic Fields vs. Dependent Origination

Aspect Sheldrake: Morphic Field Buddhism: Dependent Origination (Pratītya-samutpāda) Alignment / Divergence
Definition Invisible, formative fields that store and transmit habits/forms across space and time. Principle that all phenomena arise in dependence upon conditions; nothing has independent existence. Both reject isolated entities; one posits a field, the other a logic of conditionality.
Role of Memory Memory is non-local, accessed through resonance with past patterns. Memory is conditioned by causal chains (body, mind, karma, environment), not stored in a single locus. Both broaden memory beyond a local “storage” model.
Mechanism Hypothetical field resonance — not empirically established. Causal interdependence — metaphysical but not a substance or medium. Divergence: one suggests a hidden substrate, the other denies any underlying essence.
Transmission Habits (biological, cultural) spread through resonance, easing recurrence. Continuity arises because conditions are never isolated — causes ripple into effects without a “thing” persisting. Both describe continuity without fixed identity.
Ontology Suggests a real, non-local field structure existing in nature. Denies inherent existence — phenomena are empty, only relational. Divergence: field vs. emptiness.
Metaphor A “memory-field” shaping organisms and culture. “Indra’s Net” — infinite jewels each reflecting all others; nothing stands alone. Both use imagery of interconnectedness.
Philosophical Aim To explain biological/cultural regularities outside genetics. To undermine attachment to essence and reveal liberation through insight into emptiness. Divergence: empirical vs. soteriological goal.

Both emphasize relationality and continuity over isolated existence. However, Sheldrake introduces a field-substance that carries memory, whereas Buddhism emphasizes emptiness and dependent co-arising without positing any hidden substrate.
